question: How hot does a propane flame in air get, and how much CO and NO does it make?
headline: Adiabatic flame temperature 2266 K (1992 C) for propane in air at an equivalence ratio of 1, with 1.25% CO and 0.234% NO at equilibrium.
confidence_reasons: passed element balance, energy balance, thermo data, no dissociation bound

checks.name: element balance
checks.summary: every element of the reactants is in the products to 6e-16

checks.name: energy balance
checks.summary: the products at 2266 K hold the reactants' enthalpy to 2e-09 of cp T

checks.name: thermo data
checks.summary: GRI-Mech 3.0's own thermodynamic data give 2266 K for the same flame, 0.0694 K from NASA's (0.0031% apart)

checks.name: no dissociation bound
checks.summary: burning completely to CO2 and H2O with nothing breaking apart would reach 2392 K, and dissociation takes 126 K off it

checks.name: flammability
checks.summary: propane burns in air from 2.1% to 9.5% by volume, an equivalence ratio of 0.51 to 2.50, and this mixture is 4.03% fuel

assumptions: Propane (C3H8) and air as O2 + 3.76 N2 at 298 K and 101 kPa, fully mixed.

Adiabatic and at constant pressure, with the products in chemical equilibrium on NASA's thermodynamic data (McBride, Gordon and Reno, NASA TM-4513). A real flame loses heat by radiation and to walls, so its peak runs below this temperature.
Equilibrium NO is an upper bound on what a flame makes, since forming NO takes longer than most flames last.
